title: Trie Applications
summary: Autocomplete, Word Search II, shortest-root replacement, and maximum-XOR pairs are all the same prefix-tree trick applied differently. See where a trie beats a hash map outright.

slides.markdown:
[trie-construction-and-operations](trie-construction-and-operations) covered the mechanics: node design, insert, search, delete. This topic is about recognizing when a problem is **prefix-shaped** enough to reach for a trie in the first place.

Four patterns recur across interviews: collecting everything under a prefix (autocomplete), pruning a brute-force search using a shared dictionary (Word Search II), finding a list's longest common prefix instantly, and — the pattern that surprises people — walking a trie built over **bits** instead of characters to solve maximum-XOR problems.

The unifying skill isn't memorizing four algorithms; it's recognizing "a hash map can't answer this in one query" and reaching for the structure that can.

slides.sectionTitle: What tries solve that a hash map can't
slides.markdown:
A hash map answers one question well: "is this exact key present?" It cannot answer "does any key start with `X`" without scanning every key — hashing throws away the structure a prefix query needs.

A trie preserves that structure: every prefix of every stored key is a real, walkable node. That's why autocomplete, spell-check, and IP-routing longest-prefix-match all reach for tries rather than hash maps — the *operation itself* only makes sense on a structure that keeps prefixes addressable.

The tell in an interview: if the problem says "starts with," "prefix," "suggestions as you type," or "shortest replacement root," a trie is very likely the intended structure, even if the problem statement never says the word.

Autocomplete is two steps: walk down to the node representing the typed prefix, then DFS every path below it, collecting a full word whenever you cross a node marked `is_end`.

The walk to the prefix node is O(prefix length); the DFS afterward is O(number of matching words × their average length), since you only ever explore the subtree that actually shares the prefix — everything outside it is never touched. That's the whole efficiency story: a hash map would need to test every stored key against the prefix, while the trie physically groups matching keys together.

slides.sectionTitle: Word Search II: pruning the board with a shared trie
slides.markdown:
Word Search II asks: given a letter grid and a dictionary of words, find every word that can be traced through adjacent cells. The naive approach runs a fresh board DFS per dictionary word — if the dictionary has 1000 words, that's 1000 independent searches, each redoing work the others already did.

The trie fix: build one trie from the whole dictionary, then run a **single** DFS over the board that walks the trie alongside the board path. At each cell, only recurse into neighbors whose letter exists as a child of the *current trie node* — the trie itself prunes branches that can't possibly extend into any dictionary word, shared across all words simultaneously.

slides.sectionTitle: One search per word is the trap
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to reuse a single-word board-search helper and call it once per dictionary word — it's simpler code, and it's correct. It's also the difference between a solution that passes and one that times out.

Running the board DFS separately per word means every word re-explores overlapping cells from scratch, with no sharing of the pruning work. Building one trie up front and running **one** combined DFS means the moment a path can't extend into *any* remaining word, every word's search is pruned there simultaneously — the shared structure is the entire point, and skipping it defeats the trie's purpose in this problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Longest common prefix via first branch
slides.markdown:
Insert every word in a list into a trie, then walk from the root as long as each node has **exactly one child** and isn't itself a word end. The path you traced out is the longest common prefix of the entire list — the moment a node branches into two or more children, no word can share a longer prefix than what you've walked so far.

This costs O(total characters inserted), a single pass, versus a naive pairwise comparison of every word against every other, which is far more expensive for a large list.

The pattern generalizes past characters: a **binary trie** stores each number as a fixed-length path of bits (say 32 levels, most-significant bit first), so two numbers share a path exactly as long as their bit prefixes match.

For "maximum XOR of any pair in an array," insert every number's bit path into the trie. Then for each number, walk the trie greedily trying to go the **opposite** bit at every level — XOR is maximized by mismatched bits, so at each level you prefer the child that differs from your current bit, falling back to the same-bit child only if the opposite doesn't exist. Track the best result across all numbers.

This runs in O(n × bit-width) — for 32-bit integers, effectively O(32n), which beats the O(n²) pairwise brute force by orders of magnitude on large arrays.

slides.sectionTitle: Trie vs hash set for prefix queries
slides.markdown:
| Query | Hash set | Trie |
|---|---|---|
| Exact membership | O(L) average | O(L) |
| "Does any key start with X?" | O(n·L) — must scan all keys | O(L) |
| Collect all keys with prefix X | O(n·L) | O(L + matches) |
| Maximum XOR pair | O(n²) pairwise | O(n × bit-width) via binary trie |

A hash set physically discards prefix structure the moment it hashes a key — there is no way to answer "starts with" without falling back to a scan. A trie keeps every prefix addressable as a real node, which is exactly the structure autocomplete, Word Search II's pruning, and maximum-XOR all exploit.
